The described specimen is exempt from further infectious substance regulations, and there is no limit to the quantity of exempt human or animal specimens that can be transported per package, regardless of the mode of transport. 2. A basic triple packaging system is required for infectious substances, consisting of three layers: a primary receptacle, a secondary container, and an outer packaging. The primary receptacle must be leakproof for liquids or sift-proof for solids, appropriately labeled, and resistant to puncture, breakage, or corrosion from the infectious substance or preservation media. 3. If the infectious substance is liquid or semi-liquid, the primary receptacle must be wrapped in sufficient absorbent material to contain all fluid in case of leakage or breakage. 4. The secondary container must be watertight, leakproof, or sift-proof and must enclose and protect the primary receptacle and its absorbent material. Multiple primary receptacles can be placed in one secondary container if they contain infectious substances of the same class. Fragile primary receptacles must be individually wrapped or separated to prevent contact, with cushioning material used as needed. 5. The outer packaging must protect the secondary container from physical damage during transit. It must be strong enough to support the weight, size, and composition of the inner packages and have at least one surface with minimum dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm. 6. Specimen data forms, letters, and other documentation identifying the infectious substance should be placed between the secondary container and the outer packaging. These documents may be taped to the secondary container if necessary. 7. Packing instruction P650 provides detailed triple packaging requirements for Category B infectious substances (UN 3373). Packages compliant with P650 are considered safe for all modes of transport and are exempt from additional UN model regulation requirements, such as detailed testing and approval processes required for Category A substances. 8. P650-compliant packaging materials are generally available from local manufacturers or suppliers, who should provide clear instructions for proper use to ensure compliance. There is no comprehensive list of P650-compliant suppliers, but online searches using terms like UN packaging or UN infectious substance packaging can yield results. 9. For air transport, the primary receptacle must not exceed 1 L, and the outer packaging must not exceed 4 L of material, excluding coolants like dry ice or liquid nitrogen. For surface transport, there are no quantity limits per package. 10. Packing instruction P620 outlines the requirements for Category A infectious substances, including additional provisions beyond the basic triple packaging system. The primary receptacle must withstand internal pressure of 95 kPa and temperatures from -40°C to +55°C. It must have a secure closure, such as a heat seal or metal crimp seal, and may include flame-sealed glass ampoules or rubber-stopped glass vials. 11. The secondary container for Category A substances must also withstand 95 kPa pressure and the same temperature range. The outer packaging must be rigid, with minimum external dimensions of 100 mm, and include an itemized list of contents between the secondary and outer layers. 12. When transporting unknown infectious substances suspected to meet Category A criteria, the label must include suspected Category A infectious substance in parentheses after the proper shipping name. 13. Packaging for Category A substances must undergo rigorous testing, including drop, stacking, puncture, pressure, water spray, and temperature tests, to verify material quality. These tests are typically conducted by specialized manufacturers under quality assurance programs overseen by competent authorities. 14. Approved Category A packaging is marked with the UN packaging symbol and a series of identifiers, including the type of packaging, year of manufacture, competent authority, and manufacturer’s code. 15. For air transport, Category A substances are limited to 50 mL or 50 g per package on passenger aircraft and 4 L or 4 kg per package on cargo-only aircraft. There are no quantity limits for surface transport. 16. Medical or clinical waste containing Category B infectious substances is assigned to UN 3291 and must meet the packaging requirements of the UN Model Regulations P621. These packages do not require triple-layer packaging but must conform to Packing Group II performance levels, with sufficient absorbent material for liquids. 17. Coolants, such as dry ice or liquid nitrogen, are often used to maintain low temperatures during transport. Packaging must maintain integrity at the coolant’s temperature, and handlers must be trained in coolant safety. Ventilation safety procedures are critical, especially for air transport, to prevent pressure buildup. 18. Wet ice is not classified as a dangerous good but requires leakproof outer packaging to prevent water leakage as it melts. 19. Dry ice, classified as a Class 9 dangerous good, must be packaged to allow carbon dioxide gas release to prevent pressure buildup. Packaging must include materials like Styrofoam and follow ventilation safety procedures. 20. Liquid nitrogen, classified as a Class 2 dangerous good, is assigned the shipping name Nitrogen refrigerated liquid (UN 1977). Dry shippers, which absorb liquid nitrogen into porous material, are exempt from additional dangerous goods requirements but must be appropriately marked and labeled. 21. Stabilizers, such as sorbitol, fetal bovine serum, alcohols, or formaldehydes, may be included with infectious substances to maintain viability or prevent degradation. Small quantities of dangerous goods used as stabilizers are permitted under P620 or P650 without additional regulatory requirements. 22. Overpacks, used to consolidate multiple packages into a single handling unit, must comply with all applicable regulations, including those for coolants like dry ice.
